generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, a psychology essay is one connected act of critical writing. As you draw several studies into an argument about a disputed effect, you are already judging which evidence is more secure, and your wording carries that judgement. Setting a well-controlled study against a weaker one is synthesis, judgement and language working together, not three separate tasks.
generatedProse.worked-example: Two psychology students write about two competing studies. One reports each study in turn, then adds that one seems stronger, but never says why in the field's terms. The other synthesises them into an argument, judges the better-controlled study more secure, and uses terms like 'confound' and 'effect size' so the reasoning is visible.
generatedProse.summary: In psychology, critical writing means the three moves working as one. You synthesise several studies into an argument, judge which evidence is more secure, and word it in the field's own terms. It is the three together that turn a literature review into a critical argument of your own.

check.body: A student writes an essay that draws three sources into an argument, reaches a judgement about which view is stronger, and words it so each step is clear. What does this show?

items.text: Their next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following report improved.
Nothing; feedback comes at the end, so it cannot affect anything that follows.
Only the mark on the first report, which cannot now change.
The deadline for the next report.

feedback.correct: That's right. Using the feedback fed back into the next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following report improved: that is the cycle working.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the student changed before the next report, not the old mark or the deadline.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Using the feedback fed back into the student's next round of learning and preparation, which is why the next report improved. The old mark cannot change and the deadline is not part of the cycle; feedback is not the end, it feeds the next turn.

_items.text: That critical writing works as one practice: the argument, the judgement and the wording all do their work in the same piece.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three moves ran together in one connected act of writing.

_items.text: That the student used too many sources for one essay.
_items.feedback: The number of sources is not the point. The three moves worked together.

_items.text: That only strong students can write this way.
_items.feedback: This is something you can practise, whatever your starting point.

_items.text: That precise wording is the only move that matters.
_items.feedback: Wording carries the judgement, but the argument and judgement matter too.
